tldr: By treating most of the wound tape as a rigid body while placing an advancing deformable collar near the peel front, the authors developed a method to simulate adhesive tape dispensing, sticking, and cutting both accurately and quickly.
hero_caption: Validation of the physical behavior and core features of adhesive tape. (a) 180-degree peel force calibration between the physical setup and simulation, (b) tape dispensing from the wound rigid cluster through the deformable collar to the free strip, and (c) tape cutting triggered by blade contact pressure.
overview:
Robotic tasks involving adhesive tape—such as securing wire harnesses or sealing cardboard boxes—are in high demand. Yet, simulating tape manipulation has been surprisingly difficult. When pulling a flexible tape end, the entire roll rotates and moves while layer upon layer peels off to dispense new tape, which then reattaches to another object. If you try to solve this directly with existing finite element methods or contact simulators, computing dozens of tightly adhering contact interfaces becomes so expensive that the solver struggles to converge. At practical solver tolerances, roll rotation can completely freeze up. Conversely, if you make the entire roll permanently rigid, it cannot undergo the deformation needed to unwind and dispense tape.

To solve this, the authors noticed that most of the interior of a roll moves together almost like a single rigid body, and severe deformation only happens right at the peeling front. Their proposed method, TapeSim, groups most of the roll's interior into a single rigid cluster and places a mesh-based deformable "collar" only at the peel front. As the tape is pulled, elements dynamically switch roles: rigid elements turn into collar elements, and collar elements become part of the flexible free strip as the peel front advances. They also introduced Releasable Bonds, which simplify expensive cohesive contact interfaces.

In experiments with a 32-turn roll, this approach achieved a 3.2x to 8.4x speedup over a conventional full-shell baseline. It also showed high agreement with real-robot experiments in replaying motions and evaluating policies for lifting, sticking, and wrapping tasks, and successfully demonstrated a continuous cardboard box sealing sequence.
contributions: Proposed a model reduction method that balances rotation, deformation, and dispensing of a thin-shell tape by treating most of the wound tape as a rigid cluster and placing an advancing deformable collar at the peel front.
Introduced and evaluated Releasable Bonds, which approximate contact, friction, and peeling energy at adhesive layers using a single virtual tetrahedral element to speed up computation.
Built a simulator integrating tape adhesion, dispensing, and blade cutting, enabling real-robot motion replay and trained policy evaluation (Real-to-Sim).

sections.heading: Why is adhesive tape simulation so difficult?
sections.summary: Tape manipulation combines flexible strip deformation, overall roll rotation and translation, dispensing through layer-to-layer peeling, and reattachment to objects. Existing methods were either too computationally expensive or hit a wall where the roll would not rotate or dispense.
sections.details:
To automate wire harness securing or package sealing with robots, simulation replays and policy evaluations are essential. While simulations of rigid bodies, cloth, and ropes are actively researched, adhesive tape poses unique challenges.

When pulling the end of the tape, the roll must rotate and translate smoothly while dispensing tape, all while existing bonded surfaces stay stuck. If this coupled response is inaccurate, camera-based robot actions and task success rates will be severely thrown off.

However, trying to solve every layer of the wound tape faithfully as a thin shell produces extremely stiff systems of equations due to contact and strong cohesive forces between adjacent layers. At practical solver tolerances, roll rotation is numerically locked. If you try to increase precision, computation times skyrocket. On the other hand, if you fix the roll as a permanent rigid body, the deformation needed to pull out tape simply cannot occur.

This is where the authors made a key observation: most of the wound roll's interior moves together as a rigid body, and deformation is only fundamentally required at the peeling front. Based on this insight, TapeSim combines a rigid cluster with an advancing deformable collar to achieve both high speed and physical fidelity.

sections.heading: The intersection of deformable manipulation, adhesive contact, and reduced simulation
sections.summary: This section reviews prior work in deformable robotics, IPC-based contact and adhesion models, and reduced-order simulations like rigidification. TapeSim builds on these ideas by tailoring model reduction to the peel front and introducing simplified bonded interfaces for tape manipulation.
sections.details:
This work connects to three main areas of research.

### Robotic Manipulation of Deformables and Adhesives
Benchmarks exist for manipulating ropes, cloth, and bags, but tape adds the challenges of dispensing and reattaching. While past work explored automation using specialized jigs or planned placements assuming a taut, straight strip, dynamic simulation where tape sequentially unwinds from a freely moving roll and reattaches has remained out of reach.

### Adhesion and Contact Mechanics
Incremental Potential Contact (IPC), which strictly guarantees non-penetration, is widely used for deformable contact. Prior studies have extended IPC to adhesive contact or used the Raous–Cangemi–Cocou (RCC) model to couple contact, friction, and adhesion. TapeSim builds upon these foundations while replacing internal interfaces with lightweight virtual bonds.

### Reduced-Order Simulation Techniques
Techniques like Affine Body Dynamics (ABD) handle near-rigid objects efficiently, and adaptive rigidification dynamically toggles between deformable and rigid states. TapeSim is unique in that it switches between rigid and deformable regions specifically tailored to the physical phenomenon of the tape peeling front.

sections.heading: A clever formulation: rigid clusters, advancing collars, and releasable bonds
sections.summary: Based on thin shells and IPC, this method introduces virtual tetrahedral bonds to simplify adhesive interfaces, a rigid cluster that reduces the roll interior to 6 degrees of freedom, an advancing collar that restores deformability at the peel front, and a pressure-threshold blade-cutting mechanism.
sections.details:
TapeSim's algorithm blends high-precision contact computation with bold model reduction.

### III-A Thin-Shell Simulation with IPC
The tape substrate is modeled as a triangulated thin shell with StVK membrane elasticity and discrete shell bending elasticity. Because its rest configuration is flat, it stores elastic strain energy when wound into a roll. At each time step $\Delta t$, the solver minimizes an objective function consisting of inertia, elastic potential, normal contact barriers, and friction. IPC's barrier energy completely prevents mesh self-intersections and penetrations.

### III-B From Cohesive Contact to Releasable Bonds
Traditional cohesive contact models (based on RCC) track adhesion intensity $\beta \in [0, 1]$ across contact pairs, resisting both normal separation and tangential sliding. However, because almost no relative motion occurs at interfaces inside the roll, this computation is largely wasted.
To fix this, the authors introduced Releasable Bonds: virtual tetrahedra formed between a contact point and the three vertices of the opposing triangle, approximating adhesion, contact, and friction through their strain energy. This adds zero extra degrees of freedom and dramatically lightens computation. A bond breaks only when tensile force exceeds a threshold $f_{\rm break}$, remaining intact under compression. Once broken, the vertices revert to standard IPC contact handling.

### III-C Rigid Wound Region and the Advancing Deformable Collar
The tape is divided into three zones: a rigid cluster $\mathcal{C}$ for most of the roll's interior, a flexible deformable collar $\mathcal{L}$ around the peeling front, and a free-strip shell $\mathcal{F}$ for the dispensed portion.
Vertices inside the cluster have no individual degrees of freedom; they simply share the cluster's overall translation and rotation (6 degrees of freedom). This drastically slashes the degrees of freedom and eliminates internal contact computations.

The key mechanism is the collar's advancement. At the end of each step, the system monitors deformation $g_i = \|x_i - \tilde{x}_i\|$ (deviation from rigid motion) for collar vertices adjacent to the free strip. Once this deviation exceeds a threshold $\delta$ and the adhesion releases, the vertex is promoted to the free strip $\mathcal{F}$. Then, to maintain a collar width of $N$ edges, adjacent vertices from the rigid cluster are restored back into the deformable collar. This baton-pass allows smooth tape dispensing.

### III-D Cutting the Free Strip
Blade cutting triggers the moment local contact pressure, calculated from IPC normal contact forces between the blade and tape, exceeds a threshold (1 kPa) for two consecutive steps. The mesh is split by removing a finite-width kerf along the cutting line, allowing both resulting pieces to continue their physical simulation seamlessly.

sections.heading: Performance in real-robot comparisons, speedups, and policy evaluations
sections.summary: The authors evaluated four model variants across rigid vs. full-shell representations and cohesive vs. bond interfaces. Clustering achieved up to an 8.4x speedup on a 32-turn roll, while demonstrating high agreement with physical robots in open-loop motion replays and closed-loop policy predictions.
sections.details:
The evaluation compared four models: Coh-F (full shell, cohesive), Bond-F (full shell, bond), Bond-R (rigid cluster, bond), and Coh-R (rigid cluster, cohesive).

### IV-A Physical Setup and Core Capabilities
First, simulation parameters were tuned to match a physical 180-degree peel force measured from a table with a force gauge (median 2.54 N). When pulling a 32-turn Bond-R roll, the collar tracked properly to dispense 370.5 mm of tape over 17.75 seconds without failure, and blade cutting executed reliably.

### IV-B Roll Motion and Computational Efficiency
In swing tests where the tape end was fixed and the roll allowed to swing, solver tolerances suppressed roll rotation in the full-shell model (Coh-F). In contrast, rigid clustering (R models) restored natural, free rotational motion.
In terms of computation speed, clustering provided a 3.2x to 3.4x speedup per step on a 32-turn roll. When comparing solver tolerances needed to achieve equivalent rotational accuracy, Coh-R was 8.4x faster than Coh-F, and Bond-R was 4.5x faster than Bond-F.

### IV-C Open-Loop Motion Replay Accuracy (Stick replay)
The team replayed real-robot trajectories where an arm grips the tape end, lifts it, and sticks it onto a stand. Measuring tracking error of the roll's center landmark in camera images revealed that clustered models actually followed the real trajectory more closely: Coh-R had an error of 17.57 px (23% reduction) and Bond-R had 16.28 px (29% reduction), compared to 22.96 px for the full-shell Coh-F.

### IV-D Closed-Loop Policy Success Prediction
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies trained via imitation learning were run both on the physical robot and in simulation to test whether task outcomes matched.
- **Peel**: Rigid clustering improved agreement with real outcomes from 69% to 81–82%, and boosted Balanced Accuracy (BA) from 50% to 72.9–76.3%.
- **Stick**: Overall success rates matched well between the physical setup (70.4%) and simulation (around 68–69%), while Bond-F achieved the highest trial-by-trial balanced accuracy at 64.6%.
- **Wrap**: For predicting a single wrap, Coh-R achieved a BA of 76.6%, though predicting the more challenging two-wrap task remained difficult across all models.

### IV-E Sensitivity to Adhesive Strength
Altering table adhesion by factors of 20x and 100x caused drastic shifts in policy success rates, proving how critical prior peel force calibration is.

### IV-F Teleoperated Cardboard Box Sealing Demo
The authors demonstrated an end-to-end packing sequence: closing flaps, sticking tape, dispensing, cutting with a blade, and pressing down to seal. On an RTX 5090, the simulation ran stably at about 0.422x real-time speed.

sections.heading: Takeaways and future directions
sections.summary: TapeSim dramatically speeds up and improves the accuracy of tape dispensing simulations by pairing a rigid cluster with a dynamic collar. The authors recommend rigid clustering as the primary formulation and provide guidelines on choosing interface models depending on task requirements.
sections.details:
This paper presented TapeSim, a simulator that efficiently and accurately solves the physical behavior of wound adhesive tape.

By coupling a rigid cluster with an advancing deformable collar, TapeSim achieved a 3x to 8x+ speedup on a 32-turn roll while eliminating the numerical rotation lock observed in previous models. Comparisons against real-world robots confirmed improvements in both open-loop motion tracking and closed-loop policy evaluation accuracy.

As a practical guideline, the authors recommend using rigid clustering (R) as standard. For interface modeling, Bond-R is ideal when speed is paramount, while Coh-R is better suited for tasks involving complex re-contact, like wrapping. The upcoming source code release is expected to accelerate research into industrial robotic automation for packaging and wire harness assembly.

takeaways: Dividing roles locally—keeping the inactive interior rigid while leaving only the peeling front deformable—brings dramatic speedups and numerical stability to multilayer adhesive simulations.
Numerical solver tolerances can physically lock roll rotation; model reduction via clustering fundamentally resolves this numerical artifact.
Evaluating trial-by-trial agreement (Balanced Accuracy) is essential, rather than just matching overall simulator and real-world success rates.
limitations: In challenging tasks like Wrap with two or more turns, simulation still struggles to accurately catch rare real-world successes, leading to false negatives and false positives.
Tape peel parameters rely on prior physical calibration; deviations in adhesive strength cause rapid divergence in policy evaluation accuracy.
